title: Restarting the Speedrun Soon!? | Sicilian - Najdorf | GM Naroditsky's Theory Speedrun

moves.spoken: We take Black and play the Sicilian, c5.
We continue with d6, heading for the Najdorf.
The centre opens — we take on d4, White recaptures with the knight, and we develop to f6: a mainline Najdorf at last.
White develops the knight to c3 and we play the Najdorf move, a6.
White plays the early f3 — the English Attack.
We strike in the centre with e5.
White retreats the knight to b3. In the English Attack White typically follows with the bishop to e3, the queen to d2, castles long, and storms the kingside with pawns.
We develop the bishop to e6.
White develops the bishop to e3.
We play the bishop to e7. Normally this is the classic opposite-wing race — Black on the queenside, White on the kingside.
But White chooses the modest bishop to e2 — not dangerous; combining f3 with kingside castling is slightly weakening, though far from fatal.
We develop the knight to d7 — the customary Najdorf square; the knight rarely goes to c6 here, for positional reasons.

The plan: White has mixed the quiet Karpov bishop-e2 with the English Attack's f3 — a mishmash that hands us comfortable play. We improve with the rook to c8 and the thematic ...b5, watching for a4. If White jumps a knight to d5, we take, and after the recapture drop the bishop to f5, keeping the bishop pair; then reroute it to g6 and roll our kingside pawns — a reverse English Attack, where we attack White's king and slot in ...a4 as prophylaxis against White's queenside play. As a King's-Indian player, attacking the enemy king suits us perfectly.

A theory note: the main tabiya runs with ...Be6 and White's bishop to b3; against the sharper setups the topical ...Nbd7 leads to the wild g4 ...b5 g5 ...b4 races, though the offbeat ...a5, sending the a-pawn up the board, scores well even against grandmasters in blitz.
